First, analyze the binary => head and tail

xxd digits.bin | head -n 10

┌─[ff02x9e@parrot]─[~/picoCTF/temp]
└──╼ $xxd digits.bin | head -n 10
00000000: 3131 3131 3131 3131 3131 3031 3130 3030  1111111111011000
00000010: 3131 3131 3131 3131 3131 3130 3030 3030  1111111111100000
00000020: 3030 3030 3030 3030 3030 3031 3030 3030  0000000000010000
00000030: 3031 3030 3130 3130 3031 3030 3031 3130  0100101001000110
00000040: 3031 3030 3130 3031 3031 3030 3031 3130  0100100101000110
00000050: 3030 3030 3030 3030 3030 3030 3030 3031  0000000000000001
00000060: 3030 3030 3030 3031 3030 3030 3030 3030  0000000100000000
00000070: 3030 3030 3030 3030 3030 3030 3030 3031  0000000000000001
00000080: 3030 3030 3030 3030 3030 3030 3030 3031  0000000000000001
00000090: 3030 3030 3030 3030 3030 3030 3030 3030  0000000000000000

xxd digits.bin | tail -n 10

┌─[ff02x9e@parrot]─[~/picoCTF/temp]
└──╼ $xxd digits.bin | tail -n 10
00011790: 3030 3031 3031 3030 3030 3030 3030 3030  0001010000000000
000117a0: 3031 3031 3030 3031 3031 3030 3031 3031  0101000101000101
000117b0: 3030 3031 3031 3030 3030 3030 3030 3030  0001010000000000
000117c0: 3031 3031 3030 3031 3031 3030 3031 3031  0101000101000101
000117d0: 3030 3031 3031 3030 3030 3030 3030 3030  0001010000000000
000117e0: 3031 3031 3030 3031 3031 3030 3031 3031  0101000101000101
000117f0: 3030 3031 3031 3030 3030 3030 3030 3030  0001010000000000
00011800: 3031 3031 3030 3031 3031 3030 3031 3031  0101000101000101
00011810: 3030 3031 3031 3030 3030 3030 3030 3031  0001010000000001
00011820: 3131 3131 3131 3131 3131 3031 3130 3031  1111111111011001

30 in ASCII decimal is 48 which is 0. And 31 in ASCII decimal is 1.
This should be a natural observation since if we observe the fact that the 'thing' starts with a sequence of five 3131's and ends with 5 3131's followed by 3031 3130 3031. Upon conversion we are ought to get another file of 0s and 1s but we can analyze further down because we know it will be the simpler version of the original .bin file. 

Here is a script to convert:
with open('digits.bin', 'r') as f:
    bits = ''.join(f.read().split())

b = bytearray(int(bits[i:i+8],2) for i in range(0, len(bits) - len(bits) % 8, 8))
with open('output_file.bin', 'wb') as f:
    f.write(b)

Now analyzing the output file:

┌─[ff02x9e@parrot]─[~/picoCTF/temp]
└──╼ $xxd output_file.bin | head -n 10
00000000: ffd8 ffe0 0010 4a46 4946 0001 0100 0001  ......JFIF......
00000010: 0001 0000 ffdb 0043 0008 0606 0706 0508  .......C........
00000020: 0707 0709 0908 0a0c 140d 0c0b 0b0c 1912  ................
00000030: 130f 141d 1a1f 1e1d 1a1c 1c20 242e 2720  ........... $.'
00000040: 222c 231c 1c28 3729 2c30 3134 3434 1f27  ",#..(7),01444.'
00000050: 393d 3832 3c2e 3334 32ff db00 4301 0909  9=82<.342...C...
00000060: 090c 0b0c 180d 0d18 3221 1c21 3232 3232  ........2!.!2222
00000070: 3232 3232 3232 3232 3232 3232 3232 3232  2222222222222222
00000080: 3232 3232 3232 3232 3232 3232 3232 3232  2222222222222222
00000090: 3232 3232 3232 3232 3232 3232 3232 ffc0  22222222222222..

It is a jfif file, we can now rename it as output_file.jfif, open it and get the flag.
